articles.title: Nepal flood survivor’s family relieved at dramatic rescue after 10 days trapped
articles.summary: HONG KONG — After days of waiting anxiously, Lu Haitao’s family could finally breathe a sigh of relief when the Chinese man was rescued from a tunnel in Nepal where devastating floods killed more than 1,300 people.
articles.body: HONG KONG — After days of waiting anxiously, Lu Haitao’s family could finally breathe a sigh of relief when the Chinese man was rescued from a tunnel in Nepal where devastating floods killed more than 1,300 people. Rescuers carried out Lu from a 225-meter (740-foot) hydropower tunnel and evacuated him by helicopter Saturday, 10 days after the floods. He was taken to a hospital and was in stable condition, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported. The Aug. 26 floods were likely caused by a glacier collapse and nearly 4,900 remain missing, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency. On the Tibet side of the border, 31 people died and 531 were missing, Chinese official news agency Xinhua reported Friday. Lu recalled climbing to the highest point inside the tunnel and thinking the whistles he heard from the rescue crews were in his imagination, according to audio shared by CCTV. He told a Chinese embassy staffer that the emergency personnel initially could not hear him when he shouted toward their lights. “When they shone before my eyes, I couldn’t believe it,” he said. “When they shone before my eyes, I no longer shouted. I had lost hope.” Lu Hairong, Lu’s sister in China, told state media Red Star News that she received a call about the rescue before the news emerged. But she only found it believable after seeing him in a picture in the news. Her 49-year-old brother, who is married with a son, was previously a farmer from Henan province in central China and took additional work, mainly carpentry, during his spare time. He headed to Nepal for work with a fellow villager in February, his first time working overseas, she told Red Star News. She told Cover News, another Chinese state media outlet, that Lu had not shared his exact working location and she could only watch the news sent by others in a mutual aid group for families of the missing, unable to eat or sleep well. “It’s a stroke of sheer luck amid the misfortune,” she said of the rescue. Lu’s cousin, Lu Haiqing, said her mind went blank after learning he was missing on the sixth day after the floods. She then searched for Nepal news every day and used artificial intelligence to translate Nepali to Chinese. She wept every day on her way to work, Chinese news portal Jiupai News reported. On Saturday, Lu’s cousin received a picture from his sister asking her to help confirm his identity. The man looked very similar but she needed to call another relative to help confirm, the report said. “This day has finally come,” she was quoted as saying. “There is hope when one doesn’t give up.”

articles.title: Huge wallpaper artwork on display in Aberdeen's Bon Accord Baths
articles.summary: The work by London-based artist Tod Hanson was painted in pieces in his small studio, before being assembled with tape on the pool floor.
articles.body:
Just weeks after being used as a filming set for Netflix series Dept Q, the Bon Accord Baths in Aberdeen is opening its doors to the public to show a large-scale art installation.

'Divers', by Tod Hanson, was painted in the artist's small London studio on rolls of wallpaper - the parts were then assembled and taped to the pool floor.

Locals will be able to visit the art deco venue and see the temporary installation during the first three weekends of September.

The Category B listed baths closed in 2008 due to budget cuts and have occasionally reopened for cultural and community events since Bon Accord Heritage (BAH) took it over in 2020.

It is the second time this year the venue has hosted an art exhibit, after Scottish artist Robert Montgomery displayed one of his poetic light installations in the pool during the Nuart festival in April.

The installation is a part of the citywide Doors Open Day initiative.

The exhibition was accompanied by a musical performance from six local groups on Saturday.

Alison Reid, a retired art teacher and BAH trustee, said events like this could "breathe life" into the building.

She said the team felt a bit daunted when the artist contacted them to offer the idea last year.

Hanson typically creates large-scale graphic installations and public artworks, and is possibly best known for his work with Greenpeace in the 1990s.

His imagination was captured by the Bon Accord Baths when he saw it online.

"I just thought - what an amazing building," he said.

He worked on the artwork remotely from London and used the racing lanes and tiles of the surface of the pool as his grid plan.

They also helped form the meaning of the artwork.

He explained: "I try to look at the racing lanes already in the pool and to think about how we move through life.

"How we move through restraints or how we change and morph through our journey. The patterns change along the track, but also colours change.

"So I suppose it's about journeys, but you could read it as journeys in any form."

articles.title: Israeli air attacks on Lebanon kill at least four
articles.summary: Two women killed in an air attack on Arab Salim, and two people killed in strike on Nabatieh al-Fawqa.
articles.body:
Israeli air attacks have killed at least four people and wounded 20 others in southern Lebanon in the latest Israeli escalation despite a truce.

The strikes began at dawn on Sunday and hit Nabatieh, Arab Salim, Nabatieh al-Fawqa and Kfar Reman, Lebanon’s official National News Agency (NNA) reported.

Two women were killed and six people wounded in an air attack on Arab Salim after Israeli forces issued a forced displacement order for a building in the town, NNA reported.

Lebanon’s Health Ministry reported that at least two people were killed in an Israeli air strike on Nabatieh al-Fawqa.

An air strike on Nabatieh city also destroyed a historical building owned by the brother of a Lebanese member of parliament, damaging several buildings nearby.

In Kfar Reman, an air attack destroyed the home of the town’s late former mayor. Five people were treated in Nabatieh hospitals and discharged.

Another strike hit the Sayyida Masouma Garden in the city, destroying what remained of the municipal park after it was hit the previous day.

Israel says it carried out the strikes in response to Hezbollah launching two drones towards its forces in southern Lebanon, describing the attack as a “blatant violation” by the Lebanese armed group.

Since March, when Hezbollah attacked Israel during the US-Israel war on Iran, Israel has carried out air strikes across Lebanon and launched a ground invasion. Lebanon says the attacks have killed more than 4,300 people.

Israeli forces are still operating inside a self-declared “security zone” about 10km (six miles) deep inside Lebanon.

The number of attacks has decreased since a US-Iran Memorandum of Understanding on the broader conflict in June, while Israel and Lebanon signed a framework agreement later that month.

But Lebanon still reports Israeli strikes, artillery shelling and widespread demolitions of civilian buildings in southern villages and towns.

On Friday, Israeli strikes in the country’s south and east killed four people, including an 18-year-old woman, authorities said, as Israel said it struck Hezbollah targets in response to a drone launch towards its soldiers.

Earlier this week, Israel said it had taken “operational control” of the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge near Nabatieh. Hezbollah has not commented on the announcement.

Israel is also considering pulling its troops occupying Lebanese territory closer to the Israeli border. Israeli public broadcaster Kan, citing security sources, said the military was preparing to scale back its presence and reposition three to four kilometres closer to the Israeli border, along a new “Grey Line” where outposts would be built.

That would pull troops back from parts of the “Yellow Line”, which extends north of the Litani River. The plan has not been approved by Israel’s political leadership, and the handover of territory to the Lebanese army remains unresolved, Kan said.

Hezbollah condemned Israel’s campaign, which it said was taking place amid “complete international silence and blatant American complicity”. The group reiterated its rejection of Beirut’s “fruitless direct negotiations” with Israel.

Qatar’s Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani spoke by phone with Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam on Saturday, Qatar’s Foreign Ministry said, as Doha pressed for de-escalation.

articles.title: ‘Can no longer be stopped’: AfD races towards historic win in Germany state vote
articles.summary: Europe News: Voting began in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday in a closely watched state election that could see Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) make hist.
articles.body: Voting began in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday in a closely watched state election that could see Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) make history by becoming the first far-right party to take power at state level since World War Two, with the party's 35-year-old lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund declaring its rise "can no longer be stopped".Around 1.7 million voters in the eastern German state have until 6pm (1600 GMT) to cast their ballots, with initial results expected soon after polls close. The election is being closely watched as a test of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's strategy of countering the AfD by adopting a tougher stance on migration and security.Recent polls have put the AfD at just over 40%, well ahead of Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU), who are on around 23%. The result could determine whether the AfD merely emerges as the strongest party or secures the outright majority it needs to break through the political firewall that has kept it out of government.AfD targets outright majoritySpeaking at the party's final rally in Magdeburg on Saturday evening, Siegmund said the AfD had already achieved a historic breakthrough, regardless of Sunday's result."No matter the outcome of tomorrow's election, we have already made history," said Siegmund."Because what we have started here in Saxony-Anhalt — that is currently sweeping across all of Germany — can no longer be stopped," he told the crowd.The AfD has spent months leading the polls in Saxony-Anhalt and is hoping to secure 45% or more of the vote. Siegmund has ruled out entering a coalition with mainstream parties, arguing that those parties have driven Germany into the ground over the past three decades.An outright majority would be a major breakthrough for the AfD, allowing it to govern without relying on another party and bypass the longstanding "firewall" under which mainstream parties refuse to cooperate with it.Such a result, however, remains difficult in Germany's proportional electoral system, which is designed to encourage coalition governments and make it harder for a single party to govern alone.Coalition arithmetic could decide who governsIf the AfD falls short of a majority, the CDU is expected to have the best chance of forming the next administration under incumbent state premier Sven Schulze. But the composition of any government could depend heavily on which smaller parties manage to cross Germany's 5% threshold.The Free Democratic Party, currently a coalition partner of the CDU at the federal level, is polling below the threshold, while the Social Democratic Party (SPD) is struggling to reach 10%. The far-left Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), meanwhile, is also expected to miss out despite being the only party that has not ruled out working with the AfD.Schulze remains the voters' preferred choice for state premier in opinion polls. A CDU alliance with the SPD and Greens, however, may not secure enough seats for a majority. The CDU has also ruled out cooperation with the Left Party.One possibility could therefore be a minority government led by Schulze, relying on the Left's passive support, similar to an arrangement used in neighbouring Thuringia.Weeks of coalition negotiations could follow if no party secures enough seats to govern alone.A test for Merz and a step towards 2029The election has implications beyond Saxony-Anhalt. For the AfD, a strong performance would reinforce its claim that it is no longer a protest force confined to Germany's eastern states and would provide momentum ahead of the next federal election, scheduled for 2029.The party has been classified as "far-right extremist" by the state security service. Without an outright majority, however, its ability to translate its electoral strength into government would remain constrained by the political firewall.If it does take power, the AfD has said it would push schools and cultural institutions towards more traditional values, marginalise immigrants and carry out sweeping reforms of Germany's public broadcasting system.Siegmund arrived to cast his vote in his hometown of Tangermuende on a blue Simson moped, drawing crowds of enthusiastic supporters, as voters began deciding whether the AfD's claim that its rise "can no longer be stopped" would become a political reality.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: U.S. envoys Witkoff and Kushner set to arrive in Kyiv after peace talks in Moscow
articles.summary: President Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are set to meet with Ukrainian officials in Kyiv on Sunday, a day after meeting with Russia’s Vladimir Putin in Moscow to discuss plans toward ending the war in Ukraine.
articles.body: President Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are set to meet with Ukrainian officials in Kyiv on Sunday, a day after meeting with Russia’s Vladimir Putin in Moscow to discuss plans toward ending the war in Ukraine. Both Russia and Ukraine agreed to hold off on aerial attacks on each other’s capitals to enable the U.S. visits over the weekend, bringing a brief respite in the cities, though no broader ceasefire is in place. The renewed talks are an apparent attempt to revive Washington’s bid to end the conflict, which is in its fifth year, after months in which momentum has been stalled by the Iran war. While there has been little recent movement on the front lines, the talks come ahead of a likely difficult winter in Kyiv, which is facing a critical shortage of U.S.-made interceptor missiles able to repel Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure. Sunday’s visit to Kyiv is believed to be the first to be made by Witkoff and Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, as part of the peace effort. Witkoff has visited Moscow several times, most recently holding talks with Putin at the Kremlin in January. Witkoff on Saturday appeared to strike a particularly warm tone during the meeting with Putin. In video published by Russia’s state-owned news outlet RIA Novosti, he told the Russian leader that the delegation had been reflecting on how “when we retire, we’ll have all these incredible stories and incredible memories, and yours will be right at the top of it all.” Putin, for his part, did not publicly signal any movement from his previous steep demands, which seek major concessions from Ukraine. He praised Witkoff and Kushner in the video, telling them: “I would like to say that working with you is a comfortable experience for us, and we certainly place a high level of trust in you throughout this process.” A White House official said “substantive plans for the next steps” in the effort to end the war were at the center of the talks in Moscow on Sunday. In a statement to NBC News, the official said those next steps would be announced in the coming weeks, with the U.S. delegates looking forward to “equally productive meetings” in Ukraine. They added that officials from the National Security Council, State Department and Treasury Department joined the meeting on Saturday, which lasted more than three hours. Putin aide Yury Ushakov told Russian state media on Sunday that the meeting, which included an “informal setting at the dining table,” was “substantive, constructive, extremely frank and trusting,” noting it was the eighth time the U.S. delegation has visited Russia and that Putin had extended his “best wishes” to Trump. In a nightly address on Friday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv’s goal was to have the “most constructive, substantive visit and negotiations possible with the American side.” “We need to look for real options for how to bring this war to an end,” he said, adding: “We’ll see what proposals Steve and Jared have, and what they are told about this in Moscow.” The renewed peace efforts come as Russia has ramped up its attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities with relentless bombardments, exploiting Ukraine’s shortage of air defense systems. A Russian drone on Friday hit one of the most important government buildings in Kyiv, the headquarters of Ukraine’s Security Service known as the SBU, one of the agencies involved in the execution of deep-strike operations inside Russia. In a social media post on Saturday, Zelenskyy said Russia had launched overnight strikes on Kyiv and Boryspil international airports, linking the attack to the U.S. visit. “Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the U.S. side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine,” he said. He said Kyiv had “taken note of this Russian move” and would “adjust our operation accordingly regarding Russian airspace, which has become dangerous because of our drones and missiles in the sky.” “Of course, there are and will be no threats to diplomacy from our side,” he added, writing in a separate post that Sunday’s plans for “diplomatic engagements in Kyiv, involving the U.S. team,” had been approved. He said Ukraine was “ready for a substantive conversation.” Speaking with reporters on Friday during an event in the Oval Office, Trump said Kushner and Witkoff had been doing a “great job” in their efforts on the peace process ahead of their visits to Moscow and Kyiv. “We sent them over to see whether or not we can get something done,” he said. “And there may be a good chance that we’ll do it.”

articles.title: Police slow to respond to Dover protest, says council boss
articles.summary: The "exceptionally well organised" protest "caught several agencies on the hoof", the leader says.
articles.body:
Police were slow to react to an "exceptionally well organised" protest that ground the Port of Dover to a halt for hours, a council boss has said.

Kevin Mills, who leads Dover District Council, told the BBC that demonstrators "caught several agencies on the hoof" when they arrived on Saturday.

Hundreds of masked men chanting "stop the boats" blocked roads, causing miles of tailbacks and preventing access to the port .

Kent Police is yet to comment, but cabinet minister Jonathan Reynolds said officers "did deal with it swiftly".

Mills said the force "appeared to be quite slow to keep the roads and the networks open, which is disappointing".

"The protesters knew what they were doing, I'm not sure the police did know what was going to happen," he told the BBC.

"But then I accept that the police resource is stretched."

The Labour councillor said "no-one actually knew" what was happening on Saturday morning and there "needs to be a wash-up over that".

"All in all it was a pretty traumatic day for a lot of people travelling, trying to get around their business," he said.

Mills added that the council later received complaints from villagers in Preston, where "protesters appear to have parked their vehicles before they came in".

Chris Vinson, leader of the council's Conservative group, previously said the men had "loaded into rental vans" and then travelled to the town.

Reynolds, speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, condemned the protest.

"Peaceful protest is an essential part of British life but that is not what we saw there with that kind of intimidatory behaviour," the business secretary said.

"I feel sorry for the people around Dover and the people disrupted by that."

Police have not yet commented on who was behind the demonstration, which lasted from 07:00 BST to about 11:30.

Anti-hate organisation Hope Not Hate claimed the Patriot Platform network arranged it, saying the group began meeting in July and had brought together members of anti-migrant groups from around the country.

Demonstrators told the BBC they did not want to talk to the media, although one said "send them back" and another said "stop the boats" when approached on Saturday.

Far-right activists Tommy Robinson and Danny Thomas both posted about it on X, praising those involved.

Thomas wrote: "The experience on the ground today, was the overwhelming majority of the women and local people we spoke to were thankful that people were actually doing something."

He praised protesters for showing "discipline" and said they had "stuck to the plan".

Reynolds said that Robinson and others like him were "not interested in solving genuine problems this country has".

"They want to exploit their online following and take money from the people willing to follow them online, and that's what that agenda is," he said.

"This government is about solving the problems that really make a difference to people's lives."

Great Yarmouth MP and leader of Restore Britain, Rupert Lowe, said his party "proudly stands with those peacefully protesting against illegal immigration in Dover".

In a video on X, he said wearing balaclavas was "undesirable" but "perfectly fair for people living in this Orwellian age".

articles.title: Summer House’s Carl Radke On His Top Marathon Training Essentials
articles.summary: Bravo Summer House star and Soft Bar owner Carl Radke shares his marathon training essentials. Plus, snacks he swears by for road trips from NYC to the Hamptons.
articles.body: Talking Shop is our series where we talk to interesting people about their most interesting buys. Reality star, business owner and podcaster Carl Radke is rarely sitting still. He’s currently filming Season 11 of Bravo’s Summer House on the weekends in the Hamptons; he’s hosting events at Soft Bar, his Brooklyn-based non-alcoholic bar and cafe; and he’s recording episodes of his More Life with Carl Radke podcast, all while finding time to log dozens of miles a week while training for the 2026 Berlin and New York City marathons. Radke is also celebrating the first anniversary of Soft Bar this month, where he’s fostered an impressive community of runners and reality TV fans. He even hosts a monthly run club, which includes a DJ set and alcohol-free cocktails. If you follow Radke on Instagram, you’ve probably kept up with his running journey in some capacity — he shares his daily stats from Strava to show followers what he’s up to and to stay in touch with fellow runners. Radke even recently partnered with Strava to help launch its brand-new strength features. “Here at Soft Bar, we host a ton of different fitness and wellness events. So, working with Strava, now we’re just doing something more official, which is really cool and exciting,” he says. I recently stopped by Soft Bar to catch up with Radke. He shared everything he’s incorporating into marathon training while balancing his busy schedule, and revealed all the snacks you might have even seen him eating on Summer House during road trips to the Hamptons. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. Whether he’s running, weight training, on the golf course or in the yoga studio, Radke says there’s always some sort of electrolytes in his gym bag, like Drip Drop. “It’s not all running. I have days where I’m doing some core, some leg flexibility and stretching, but I also love hot yoga, bike riding and swimming,” he says. “Electrolytes are probably my non-negotiable. I’m always starting a workout or my morning with electrolytes. I feel more clear-headed, I feel energized and I feel hydrated.” Radke is no stranger to long-distance running — he’s currently training for his second marathon of 2026 which is this month in Berlin, followed by the New York City marathon in November. Depending on his workout of the day, he swaps out his shoes of choice. “I have running shoes for long runs. I have running shoes that are maybe just for an easy short run. So depending on what activity I’m doing, I always have to have a pair of shoes I’m excited to put on,” he says. Radke also enjoys trying out new workout apparel and shoes. “If you feel good in the thing you’re wearing to workout in, I think it helps get your mind right,” he says. He was wearing the new, highly-cushioned Asics SuperBlast 3 when we spoke. As an original cast member of Bravo’s Summer House, Radke has been trekking from New York City to the Hamptons for the last 10 summers. “Every weekend — Friday, Saturday, Sunday — from the end of June until Labor Day, I’ve been doing that,” he says. He and his castmates know exactly where to stop for provisions along the way during the three to four hour drive, but he also likes to bring a few road trip snacks from home. “Anybody that knows me from our group knows that I’m the snack guy,” says Radke. These Nature Valley granola bars are one of Radke’s all-time favorites, even though he admits their crumbs get everywhere, which you’ve likely experienced if you’ve tried them yourself. Radke has been sober for almost five years, and he just celebrated the one-year anniversary of Soft Bar, his non-alcoholic bar and cafe in Brooklyn. When I asked if he has a favorite beverage for his road trips, he immediately recommended Canada Dry’s Seltzer Waters. “It’s the number one seltzer water. I don’t care what anyone says. It’s got the highest carbonation rate,” he says. Radke says working with Strava is the most no-brainer partnership he’s ever done. He’s been using the platform organically for years, and is constantly sharing his progress with his followers from all over the country. “I have folks that follow my runs in Charleston, L.A. and New York, so I’ve been able to connect [with them] on a larger scale because of the Strava platform,” he says. Although the platform is highly popular among runners, Strava extends beyond tracking jogs and walks — Radke even uses Strava to track his golf rounds on his smartwatch. The brand recently launched a new strength training experience built for those aiming to track lifting workouts, which Radke is incorporating into his marathon training routine. “My running coach has me on a weight training program in addition to running,” he says. Most strength training features are now available in the app with a free membership, and there’s an expanded range of capabilities available with a paid subscription. Why trust NBC Selected? I’m an associate social media editor leading social media and newsletter production for NBC Selected. To write this article, I interviewed Carl Radke about his Strava partnership and his favorite products. articles.title: Anti-migrant AfD seeks to break Germany’s political ‘firewall’ in historic state election
articles.summary: Young voters are fueling Germany's AfD surge in Saxony-Anhalt, where lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund has amassed over 700,000 TikTok followers.
articles.body: A political earthquake is brewing in Germany's east as working-class and young voters appear set to deliver an unprecedented victory for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in Sunday’s state elections in Saxony-Anhalt. The AfD, which was famously backed by Elon Musk in last year’s national election, has been criticized for being pro-Russia and was accused of being a "right-wing extremist endeavor" by Germany’s domestic intelligence office, has the chance to become the first party outside the mainstream center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) or center-right Christian Democratic Union and their Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), to win an outright majority in a German state parliament, or Landtag, since World War II. "The reason Saxony-Anhalt matters," foreign policy expert and author Daniel Schatz, who holds a doctorate in political science from Berlin's Humboldt University, told Fox News Digital, "is that the AfD is no longer just knocking on the door of power. It may be close to kicking it open." TENS OF THOUSANDS OF FAR-LEFT PROTESTERS CLASH WITH POLICE IN ANTI-CONSERVATIVE PARTY RIOTS Other minor parties have led governing coalitions in German states, but no party outside the SPD or the CDU and the CSU has ever held a single-party governing majority in Germany since the Federal Republic was re-established in 1949. Janek Treiber, a political science researcher at Dresden University of Technology, told Fox News Digital that if the AfD does win outright in Saxony-Anhalt, their policy influence would be limited due to the German federal system, but warned "you must not underestimate the political symbol this would give. That a single party, and a right-wing party, could rule a German state… The symbol that these parties, that have been ruling Germany since 1949 or the East since 1990, they now lose control. They now lose power. I think this is a much more important symbol than just saying, OK, (the) AfD will change this or that in its local school system or university system." Schatz described the AfD "a nationalist, anti-immigration party on the far right that has become a powerful vehicle for voter anger at Germany’s political establishment — especially in the former East Germany. It campaigns for much tighter immigration, a stronger emphasis on German national identity, rejection of much of the green agenda and a softer line toward Russia." An outright win for the AfD, even in Germany’s 6th smallest state, would break through the political establishment’s so-called "Brandmauer," or "firewall." Simply put, other parties refuse to work with the AfD, which is currently the second-largest party in the Bundestag, officially the opposition party, after winning 20.8% of the vote in the February 2025 federal election. 'SEND THEM BACK' CHANTS ROCK EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AFTER LANDSLIDE VOTE TO SPEED UP DEPORTATIONS In an interview on German broadcaster ZDF, the AfD’s national co-chair, Alice Weidel, advocated for closing Germany’s borders and exiting Europe’s Schengen treaty, saying, "Illegal migration, unchecked open borders, anyone can get in. Our internal security is suffering. People are honestly fed up with this situation." Weidel added, "All Syrian refugees must have their protected status revoked because the reason for their flight no longer exists. These people must return to their homeland. If they don't leave voluntarily, then they must be deported by force." Adding that many of the 1.3 million Syrians in Germany are being naturalized, "we must stop naturalizing these people who should actually be leaving our country. We have Islamization." GERMAN OFFICIALS WANT TO KNOW WHY BERLIN ATTACK SUSPECT WAS FREE DESPITE ALLEGED ISIS SUPPORT In May 2025, Germany's Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV) classified the AfD as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" group, citing "anti-migrant positions and an ancestry-based definition of German identity." This past February, according to Deutsche Welle, that classification was put on hold by a German court after "Judges found that while there was evidence of potentially unconstitutional statements and policies within the AfD… it said that there was not sufficient evidence to characterize the party as a whole as extremist." German Chancellor Friedrich Merz recently told state broadcaster ARD, "I cannot imagine international investors attending a ground-breaking ceremony with an AfD Minister-President to set up new plants and establish new businesses in Saxony-Anhalt… However, that is a decision for ​the voters in Saxony-Anhalt to make. The state will suffer ⁠considerable damage if things turn out as we now fear they ​might." This has done little to damage the popularity of the AfD’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund. In a state of just over 2 million people, he has a TikTok following of over 700,000. A Center for Strategic & International Studies (CSIS) report said Siegmund’s "polished appearance and professional tone lend respectability, and radical demands blend with footage of a community-oriented politician responding to audience questions… The AfD’s physical presence in the streets and omnipresence in the media helps to push the common populist ‘us versus them’ narrative: The AfD is here for you, the other parties are not." NEW GERMANY SEX-CRIME FIGURES REIGNITE MIGRATION FIGHT AS EXPLOITATION PROBE EXPANDS According to the independent, non-partisan German website Wahlrecht.de, which tracks federal and state election polling, ahead of Sunday’s vote in Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD holds a 41%-23% lead over the CDU, followed by three leftist parties. A party or a coalition needs at least half of the seats to control parliament and name a state Minister-President, essentially a governor. So how can a party with only 43% win an election outright? That comes down to Germany’s unique election system. "German voters cast two ballots," Schatz says, "One for a local candidate — like voting for your congressman - and one for a party. That second vote, the party vote, is the one that counts. It decides how many seats each party gets in parliament." But there is a caveat: "Any party that falls below 5% gets nothing — zero seats — and those votes are effectively thrown out. Right now, several smaller parties are hovering right at that line. If they miss it, 42% or 43% of the vote can translate into more than half the seats. So Saxony-Anhalt could wake up to an AfD majority government even though a clear majority of voters chose someone else. That would be a first in postwar Germany." The CSIS report said voters are drawn to the AfD "because, or despite of, its extremist ideology. 60.5% of AfD voters hold a right-wing extremist worldview… At the same time, more than two in five AfD voters think that the party does not sufficiently distance itself from right-wing extremist positions." The report also found that AfD’s "strongest recent gains have been among voters 18–25 years old, where the party tripled its results compared to the 2021 national election." Treiber said economics is pushing younger voters to the AfD, due to rising expenses and unemployment. He also said that younger voters are "kind of polarized because the other part of the youth in Germany is voting for the left party (Die Linke)." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Saxony-Anhalt may just be the beginning for the anti-establishment parties. Voters in neighboring Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where former Chancellor Angela Merkel grew up and began her political career, go to the polls in two weeks. Polling data from Wahlrecht.de shows the AfD leading the ruling SPD 35%-32% there. Conversely, in Berlin, where voters in the capital also go to the polls in two weeks, the average of recent polling has the far-left Die Linke in a dead heat with the CDU at 20%, followed by the AfD at 18%, with the Greens and the SPD each around 15%. While the majority of the AfD’s support does come from the former East Germany, the party is represented in 14 of Germany’s 16 state legislatures and holds 15 of Germany’s 96 seats in the European Parliament.

articles.title: Karmelo Anthony seeks $250K for murder appeal as questions persist over family’s previous $634K fundraiser
articles.summary: Karmelo Anthony's family launches a new $250,000 GiveSendGo appeal fund after a previous campaign raised nearly $634,000 and sparked spending questions.
articles.body: Karmelo Anthony’s family is seeking another $250,000 to fund his appeal after an earlier campaign raised nearly $634,000 and faced questions over how the money was spent, the family announced at a news conference in Dallas, Texas. The fundraising push came nearly two weeks after a judge denied Anthony’s request for a new trial. His family and supporters, including attorney Russell Wilson, used the Dallas news conference to outline the appeal. Anthony, 19, was sentenced to 35 years in prison in June after a jury convicted him of murdering 17-year-old Austin Metcalf during a high school track meet in Frisco, Texas. He has appealed and says he cannot afford to hire an attorney for the appeal. ANOTHER LAWYER JOINS KARMELO ANTHONY'S APPEAL AS KILLER CLAIMS HE CANNOT PAY FOR COUNSEL The new fund is intended to cover legal fees, experts and other costs associated with challenging Anthony’s conviction, Wilson said. articles.title: Witkoff and Kushner arrive in Kyiv for second leg of US diplomacy push
articles.summary: US envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner travelled to Kyiv on Sunday after concluding intensive talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, as Washington renews its push to end the war in Ukraine.
articles.body: US envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner travelled to Kyiv on Sunday after concluding intensive talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, as Washington renews its push to end the war in Ukraine. It marks their first visit to the Ukrainian capital since the war began and comes amid near-constant Russian missile and drone strikes on the Ukrainian capital. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said that an acute shortage of air defense interceptors has left Ukraine vulnerable to ballistic missile attacks. Zelensky said he held a meeting with his negotiating team ahead of talks with the US envoys. “We are ready for talks. Ukraine has always been and will continue to be constructive,” he wrote on Telegram. “We are committed to bringing the war to an end. Peace is needed. Security guarantees are needed. A dignified post-war peace is needed. Our proposals are ready,” Zelensky continued. Witkoff and Kushner made a stop in the Polish city of Rzeszow en route from Moscow to Kyiv, Russian state media outlet TASS reported. The plane landed at 1:31 a.m. local time. The US envoys most likely continued their journey by rail, it reported. Russia and Ukraine have enacted a 72-hour temporary truce for the duration of the US envoys’ visits, specifically halting airstrikes on each other’s capitals, Kyiv and Moscow. The halt in strikes began at midnight on Friday into Saturday and will last for the duration of the weekend of diplomacy. The truce applies only to the two capital cities, and overnight attacks into Sunday saw Russia continue its bombardment of Ukraine while avoiding Kyiv city. According to Ukraine’s Air Force, Russian forces launched 108 Shahed-type drones fired from Russia, while at least three people were killed in the latest strikes and infrastructure was hit in Kyiv region. Russian airstrikes were recorded in 11 locations across Ukraine, while a large-scale fire has been extinguished at an infrastructure facility in Kyiv region as a result of a Russian strike. In total, 10 Ukrainian civilians have been killed over the past 24 hours, and a further 65 injured. Witkoff and Kushner began their whirlwind weekend of diplomacy with a three-hour meeting with Putin at the Kremlin on Saturday afternoon. The negotiations were followed by dinner with the Russian leader, according to a Kremlin press briefing. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov later described the talks as “useful” and said the American representatives had “prepared seriously for this trip.” He said the US team expressed interest in ending hostilities as quickly as possible and offered “a whole series of considerations regarding possible paths to a settlement.” A White House official said both sides “discussed substantive plans for next steps, which will be announced in the coming weeks.”

articles.title: Hollywood star William Holden helped buy an 1,800-acre Kenyan game farm in the 1960s; it became one of East Africa's pioneering breeding projects
articles.summary: Rest of World News: William Holden was one of Hollywood's biggest stars, but some of his most lasting work happened far away from the film sets of Los Angeles. In Kenya, .
articles.body: William Holden was one of Hollywood's biggest stars, but some of his most lasting work happened far away from the film sets of Los Angeles. In Kenya, his fascination with wildlife led him to support an ambitious conservation experiment that began in the 1960s. Holden became involved in the development of a vast game ranch on the slopes of Mount Kenya, where threatened African animals could be protected and bred. The project was unusual for its time: rather than simply keeping wildlife for display, its founders wanted to create viable breeding populations that could help safeguard species disappearing from the wild. The ranch eventually became associated with pioneering work involving animals such as the mountain bongo, one of Kenya's most endangered antelopes. According to the William Holden Wildlife Foundation (WHWF), the conservation effort would later grow into a wider mission combining wildlife protection, environmental education and community outreach.William Holden's unlikely connection to KenyaHolden developed a deep attachment to Kenya after visiting the country and becoming increasingly interested in its wildlife. During the 1960s, he joined conservation-minded partners in developing the Mount Kenya Game Ranch, a large private wildlife project near Mount Kenya. The William Holden Wildlife Foundation records that the ranch became an important early experiment in African wildlife conservation, with Holden providing financial support while also remaining personally involved in the project. Its purpose went beyond creating a scenic retreat. The founders wanted to establish a protected environment where endangered and threatened animals could reproduce safely. At a time when conservation breeding was still developing, the idea was remarkably forward-looking. The ranch eventually became home to numerous African species and developed breeding programmes intended to maintain populations that could potentially support future conservation efforts.The mountain bongo became a conservation priorityAmong the animals that became particularly important to the ranch was the mountain bongo, a large, vividly marked forest antelope native to Kenya. By the 1960s, populations were under growing pressure as their forest habitat was reduced and hunting took its toll. According to historical material published by the William Holden Wildlife Foundation, Holden and ranch manager Don Hunt began a determined effort in 1967 to capture young mountain bongos and establish a secure breeding population. Over several years, 20 young animals were eventually transferred to zoos in the United States. The decision created a population outside the species' increasingly threatened natural habitat. What initially appeared to be an extraordinary intervention later proved significant. As wild mountain bongo numbers continued to decline, the animals descended from those early transfers became an important genetic reserve for future conservation and reintroduction efforts.A breeding project became a broader wildlife missionThe Kenyan ranch did not focus on a single species. Its conservation work expanded to include numerous animals, while an orphanage and rehabilitation programme provided care for young wildlife that had been abandoned or otherwise needed protection. The project reflected a growing understanding that simply protecting individual animals was not enough; conservation also required maintaining viable populations and educating people about the ecosystems supporting them. The William Holden Wildlife Foundation later built on this philosophy. Following Holden's death in 1981, his conservation legacy continued through the foundation established in his name. Its education centre was created on part of the former game ranch, bringing conservation education directly to Kenyan communities and schools. The organisation now combines wildlife protection with environmental education, biodiversity programmes and sustainable-development initiatives.William Holden's conservation legacy lives onHolden remains best known for his Oscar-winning Hollywood career, but his work in Kenya created a very different legacy. The breeding efforts at the Mount Kenya Game Ranch helped preserve animals at a time when wildlife populations were facing mounting threats. Most notably, the mountain bongo population established through animals sent overseas eventually provided the foundation for later conservation and repatriation efforts. The story demonstrates why the ranch was more than a celebrity's African retreat. It became an early example of how captive breeding, habitat protection and education could work together to protect endangered wildlife. Today, the foundation continues that broader conservation philosophy through education and environmental programmes in Kenya. Holden's greatest contribution, therefore, may not have been a film performance at all, but helping create a conservation project whose influence continued long after his death.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A play about love in London has entranced New Yorkers
articles.summary: As the cast of ‘Shifters’ prepare to take their final bow, we ask why this Black love story resonated so deeply.
articles.body: When actor Charity Bedu-Addo first read the script for “Shifters” — an intimate, Black romance conceptualized by playwright Benedict Lombe and director Lynette Linton — she knew something significant had landed in her hands. “I couldn’t put it down,” Bedu-Addo said of her initial encounter with the play ahead of its original 2024 run on London’s West End. Starting off as an understudy, Bedu-Addo now plays the female lead in an across-the-pond adaption of the Laurence Olivier Award-nominated play. “I went all the way home. I’m literally crossing traffic, couldn’t put it down. Read it all that night,” she said. Audiences have felt similar. For the last two years, the story has entranced showgoers with its heartbreaking portrayal of an imperfect love story. Bestselling authors, fervent theater-goers, and culture critics alike have all heralded the production as a special chapter in the canon of Black theater. Now, in New York, it’s common to see an audience of young and mostly Black and POC millennials exit the Cherry Lane Theatre, filled with emotion as they dissect the play on their way out. It’s refreshing to overhear how the play instantly resonates, how one’s own fears and hopes about life and love were just reflected back at them. At first glance, “Shifters” seems like a simple concept and one we’ve seen in movies such as “The Notebook,” or “Serendipity.” Two former friends-turned-lovers, Des and Dre , reconnect at a funeral, and their yearslong love story unspools into the next hour and forty minutes. In one moment, the pair are in their 30s, in another, they’ve slipped into their teenage years in the early aughts, and so on for all of the subsequent moments in between. Each vignette of time reveals how time, our upbringing, and even our individual dreams shape the path of our lives and who ultimately ends up beside us for the ride. As is common with these tales of sliding doors, the narrative isn’t linear. Through its grappling with ideas of memory and perspective, there’s a liminality that could be disorientating, but it isn’t. “When me and Bene were collaborating she used to write things like, ‘Dre disappears,’” Linton, who originally commissioned Lombe to write this Black British romance, said. “We used to joke all the time, it’s not possible. She’d write the most beautiful things, but it inspired me to then try,” “Bene is very intentional with every single thing that she’s done,” Bedu-Addo said. “There’s no accident. Each ellipsis is meant to be there. Each song is meant to be there.” The haunting opening chords to Alice Smith’s cover of “I Put A Spell On You,” with its loop effect and cued to the top of the play is proof. Awilo Longomba’s Congolese classic “Karolina,” “No One Like You” by P-Square and Skepta’s “Too Many Man” soundtracked Lombe’s writing process often illicit approving exclamations from the audience as Des and Dre swap a playlist of highly recognizable tracks for anyone who came of age in up in the 2000s. Equally, Lombe “makes it very, very easy to picture these characters, to feel what they’re feeling, to understand the layers, but also to keep them so light and so fun and so real,” said Bedu-Addo. Daniel Ezra, who plays Dre, sees the show as an invitation to remember the parts of us that may be buried in time. “I think we forget that so much of our blueprint was built before: so much of the decisions we make, the things we do, come from things that have happened or have been done before.” Ezra said. “The show does a really good job of mapping that in a very real way. I think it brings people back to that pure feeling of being in love.”

articles.title: Why some of France’s most famous cheeses are in peril
articles.summary: Historic heat waves are putting French dairy cows that normally graze outdoors in summer under heat-related stress. Prolonged periods of drought are scorching French pastures, leeching them of their usual lush green vitality and leaving behind parched, lifeless yellow fields. And French farmers bound by strict cheesemaking regulations are having to buy extra feed to supplement the animals’ diets.
articles.body: Historic heat waves are putting French dairy cows that normally graze outdoors in summer under heat-related stress. Prolonged periods of drought are scorching French pastures, leeching them of their usual lush green vitality and leaving behind parched, lifeless yellow fields. And French farmers bound by strict cheesemaking regulations are having to buy extra feed to supplement the animals’ diets. Some of France’s most beloved artisanal cheeses are under threat from the effects of climate change, scientists and cheesemakers warn. “Before, we used to have a problem with the grass every 15-20 years,” says Laurent Lours, who has been a dairy farmer and cheesemaker for 35 years. “Now, it’s about every other year. And it’s getting worse.” The result? Dairy cows are producing less milk and birthing fewer or weakened calves. Farmers who produce many of the country’s top-tier cheeses have been forced to cease production. And the distinct flavor of France’s “terroir” cheeses are at risk. “We’ve had five heat waves so far this year. We’ve never experienced temperatures like this before,” Lours says. Indeed, the month of July set a new record in France, bagging the title of hottest month since record-keeping began in 1900, and the third driest month on record, according to France’s national weather service. Strict regulations, punishing conditions This summer, more than three-quarters of France’s 80 producers of Salers cheese – a semi-hard, raw cow’s milk cheese – were brought to a standstill following a series of heat waves and accompanying drought. Salers is one of 47 French cheeses that carries the red and yellow AOP label, Appellation d’origine protégée (“protected designation of origin” in English), a certification guaranteeing that all stages of the final product — from milk production to aging — have taken place within a limited geographic area. Salers is produced mainly in the department of Cantal in the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region of southeast France, where cows graze at altitudes of between 2,630 and 4,920 feet (about 800 to 1,500 meters) above sea level on a volcanic massif, carpeted in nutrient-dense wild grasses. While no two Salers cheeses are alike, the local terroir — a mix of climate, soil, and topography that makes a region unique — produces a flavor profile that can range from walnuts, hazelnuts and grass, to fermented cream, peppery spice and smoked, grilled onion. It’s also one of the cheeses hardest hit by the impacts of climate change, as its production is subject to strict regulations: Salers must be produced between April 15 and November 15 by grazing cows that are mainly grass-fed. Supplementation to their diet is limited to no more than 25% of dry matter and permitted feed ingredients include hay, wheat, barley, oats and maize from the same region. This year’s drought forced Lours to drop production of Salers on July 8 and switch to making Cantal, a semi-hard cow’s milk cheese similar in profile but subject to laxer rules. Unlike Salers, Cantal can be produced year-round, while the grass to grain, hay and corn ratio is more generous. The main rule is that cows be able to graze 120 days of the year. Last month, the government body responsible for overseeing the AOP label, the Institut national de l’origine et de la qualité (INAO), announced temporary modifications for a selection of cheesemakers in response to France’s “historic drought” this summer. Producers of Beaufort, Comté and Abondance are among a handful of cheeses that have already been authorized to increase the share of fodder for cows to make up for the grass shortage, or source supplementary feed from outside their designated AOP zones. And the list of cheeses is expected to grow. Lours, who is also the president of the Comité interprofessionnel des fromages du Cantal and represents local cheesemakers, said their group didn’t bother requesting a temporary exemption to the rules for Salers because anything less than 50% of pasture-grown grass would not “deserve the designation” of the Salers name. For years, producers of some AOP cheeses have been asking the INAO to permanently relax some of the regulations in response to the effects of human-made climate change, be it by adjusting the grazing period, increasing the amount of hay and supplemental feed that cows can consume, and allowing farmers to source feed from outside their AOP region. The process is long and can take years to finalize. But does reducing the minimum grazing requirements impact the quality and flavor of the final product? According to a team of French researchers, it could mean the difference between a good cheese, and an insipid one. In a study conducted at France’s National Research Institute for Agriculture, Food and Environment (Institut national de recherche pour l’agriculture, l’alimentation et l’environnement or INRAE) last year, researchers fed four groups of cows different diets for four months to simulate various drought conditions. After varying the ratios of grass to hay and corn, the milk was then collected to make Cantal cheese and analyzed both in labs and by a jury of consumer experts. The findings were clear: cheese made with mostly grass-based cow milk was richer and higher in healthy omega 3 fatty acids. Moreover, the cheeses were also superior in taste, aroma, smell and texture for consumers. “When cows feed on pastured grass the cheeses are softer, yellower and more aromatic, while when they eat little or no grass the cheeses are whiter, firmer and have less pronounced tastes,” INRAE says in a statement. While the industry is very concerned about the possible effects of modified rules on its products, Christian Janier, a fourth-generation cheesemonger in Lyon, in the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region, thinks the end result is likely to be subtle and imperceptible for the average consumer. “The quality may inevitably drop a little given that we know that feed plays a major role in the final product,” he says. “But in the end, it won’t be enough for a regular consumer to notice.” Steady decline in Salers cheese production Along with affecting the quality of cheeses, climate change also poses a threat to the livelihoods of French dairy farmers and a rich cheesemaking tradition in France. Cows suffering from heat exhaustion are producing 10% less milk and losing about a month’s worth of outdoor grazing due to frequent and prolonged episodes of drought, says Lours. The drop in milk production has led to a steady decline in supply: production of Salers cheese has dropped from an average of 1,500 tons a year in the early 2010s to around 1,000 tons today, he adds. On top of that, the grass shortage forces farmers to dip into the hay supply they’ve stockpiled for use in winter. Lours says he’s already spent close to €30,000 ($35,000) on additional feed this summer. “Some producers are losing motivation as it’s getting more and more complicated. We’re losing market share, and it’s hard to stay in business, so it’s difficult.” Lours said. Stéphanie Gardes is another producer who has had to abandon the production of Salers mid-summer for the less profitable Cantal because of drought. It’s a blow, after having lost €20,000 ($23,300) last year in revenue due to similar conditions. Compared to Salers, Cantal nets cheesemakers around €3 euros less per kilo for the same amount of work, she points out. This season, production stopped earlier than usual. This is set to become her worst financial year since becoming a cheesemaker nine years ago. “Two years in a row is tough. And right now, we don’t know when it’s going to end. We can’t see the light at the end of the tunnel,” she says. “It’s demoralizing.” Other cheeses under threat Salers and Cantal are hardly the only cheeses to be impacted by the effects of repetitive heat waves and drought. Producers of a host of other AOP cheeses like Roquefort, a blue cheese made with raw sheep’s milk from Aveyron in the south, and Abondance, a semi-hard cheese produced in Haute-Savoie in the southeast, also report difficulty fulfilling the AOP grazing requirements. Every summer, Emilie Jacquot, her husband and two children escort their 50 dairy cows up into the mountains to 4,920 feet (about 1,500 meters) near Annecy, where they relocate their entire organic Abondance cheesemaking operation and set up camp in the family’s mountain chalet for three months. This year marked the first time they didn’t have to light a fire in their wood-burning stove in the chalet to keep warm, she says. During the rest of the year, in the valley below, Jacquot says climate change has also contributed to wild temperature swings, which can range from 23 degrees Fahrenheit to 77 degrees (minus 5 Celsius to 25 Celsius) in a single day. “We see global warming throughout the whole year,” Jacquot says. “In the summer we have heat waves, but in winter we can have huge temperature fluctuations over the course of the day. That’s what’s hard to deal with.” The forces affecting cheese quality Not unlike wine, some seasons yield better cheeses than others, with factors that extend beyond heat and drought, says the cheesemonger Janier. Climate change also drives more intense rainfall, and when cows graze on rain-soaked grass, they produce “moist milk,” a term to describe milk that is lower in protein. Cheeses made with moist milk mature faster and can develop unpleasantly pungent odors and flavors like ammonia. “Once cheese has reached its peak, it’s like wine, the quality starts to go downhill. Just like human beings,” he quips. Janier jokes that he was born in a cheese vat and that milk runs through his veins. He is also one of only seven cheesemongers in the country who are certified Meilleurs Ouvriers de France or MOF, a national-level distinction that recognizes the country’s best crafts people and artisans through a rigorous competition. Janier laments what he describes as the “standardization” of French cheeses over the years, driven in large part by industrial mass-production. “We have fewer cheeses that are terrible, but also fewer cheeses that are truly excellent,” he says. But while climate change continues to put pressure on the industry, the AOP label remains the surefire way to identify a high quality cheese, Janier adds. “As soon as a cheese has a AOP stamp, you know that it’s passed a host of tests for texture, aroma and flavor.”
